questions.q: In `summarize FailedCount = count(), LastFailure = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)`, what does `bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)` do?
options: Deletes rows older than 10 minutes
Rounds each timestamp down into fixed 10-minute buckets, so failures group by both user and time window
Counts how many users signed in during the last 10 minutes
Converts TimeGenerated into IP addresses
questions.explain: bin() rounds a datetime down into fixed-size buckets, which is what lets summarize group failures by user AND by a specific 10-minute window rather than across all time.

questions.q: Why isn't the simple failure-count query (`FailedCount > 5`) enough on its own to detect the pattern this rule targets?
options: Because it runs too slowly against SigninLogs
Because it fires on any user with 5+ failures regardless of whether a success ever followed, so it isn't sequence-aware of the specific "failures then success" pattern
Because KQL doesn't support summarize on SigninLogs
Because it only works for Linux servers
questions.explain: A count-only query can't distinguish "failures then a success" from "failures with no success at all" — it's missing the order-sensitive check the join adds.

questions.q: What does `join kind=inner Successes on UserPrincipalName` combined with `where SuccessTime > LastFailure and SuccessTime < LastFailure + 10m` accomplish?
options: It deletes all failed sign-in records
It keeps only cases where a successful sign-in landed after a user's failure cluster and within a reasonable window of it — making the query sequence-aware
It counts distinct IP addresses per user
It disables the account automatically
questions.explain: This is exactly the piece that turns a plain failure-count into a real "failures, then a success" detection — checking that the success happened after, not just that both occurred.

questions.q: Why does the rule set "Lookup data from the last" to 20 minutes when it runs every 10 minutes?
options: Because Sentinel requires lookback to always be double the run frequency
To absorb log ingestion delay — an event just before a run that hasn't finished ingesting yet could otherwise fall into a gap between two runs
Because KQL queries can't run on windows shorter than 20 minutes
To reduce the number of alerts generated
questions.explain: Setting the lookback window longer than the run frequency is the standard way to avoid missing events that are still being ingested right at the boundary between two scheduled runs.

questions.q: What does mapping `UserPrincipalName` to the Account entity and `IPAddress` to the IP address entity actually enable?
options: It makes the query run faster
It lets Sentinel correlate this alert with any other alert touching the same account or IP address, instead of leaving it as an isolated match
It automatically blocks the IP address
It's required for the query to compile
questions.explain: Entity mapping is what makes an alert investigable — without it, Sentinel has no way to link this match to other activity involving the same user or address.
